sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Regulating Act of 1773**: Created the office of **Governor-General of Bengal** and an executive council of four members to assist **Warren Hastings**, ending the corruption-laden **Dual Government** system.
• **Pitt's India Act of 1784**: Reduced the executive council size to three members, established the **Board of Control** in London to exercise political control over the Company, and subordinated Madras and Bombay presidencies entirely to Bengal.
• **Charter Act of 1833**: Renamed the Governor-General of Bengal as the **Governor-General of India**, centralizing complete legislative and financial powers for all British territories in India under **Lord William Bentinck**.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: Gradual transition from a profit-seeking mercantile corporation to a sovereign imperial administrative state, financed through aggressive land revenue extractions like the Permanent Settlement.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: Warren Hastings (1774–1785)
Regulating Act 1773, abolition of Dual Govt, Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774), Diwani and Faujdari Adalats.
First Anglo-Maratha War, Second Anglo-Mysore War, Rohilla War, Treaty of Salbai, Treaty of Mangalore.
Impeachment trial in British Parliament; foundation of civil services and revenue administration.
Lord Cornwallis (1786–1793)
Permanent Settlement of Bengal (1793), Cornwallis Code (separation of revenue and justice), establishment of Civil Services & Police.
Third Anglo-Mysore War, Treaty of Seringapatam, defeat of Tipu Sultan.
Father of Civil Services and Police in India; institutionalized Europeanization of higher services.
Sir John Shore (1793–1798)
Policy of Non-Intervention, Charter Act of 1793.
Battle of Kharda (1795) between Nizam and Marathas.
Classic case study of the failure of non-intervention leading to regional instability.
Lord Wellesley (1798–1805)
Introduction of Subsidiary Alliance System.
Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, Second Anglo-Maratha War, Treaty of Bassein.
Aggressive imperial expansion; transformation of Company into paramount power.
Lord George Barlow (1805–1807)
Adherence to non-intervention policy, Vellore Mutiny (1806).
Suppression of the Vellore Mutiny.
First major military mutiny by Indian sepoys against social/religious interference.
Lord Minto I (1807–1813)
Charter Act of 1813 (ended Company trade monopoly except tea and China), Treaty of Amritsar (1809) with Ranjit Singh.
Diplomatic missions to Lahore, Kabul, and Persia to counter French threat.
Shift in British policy toward Central Asia and legal formalization of Christian missionary entry.
Lord Hastings / Earl of Moira (1813–1823)
Ryotwari system (formalized in Madras/Bombay), abolition of Peshwaship.
Anglo-Nepal (Gorkha) War (Treaty of Sagauli), Third Anglo-Maratha War, suppression of Pindaris.
Ended the policy of non-intervention and established absolute British supremacy in India.
Lord Amherst (1823–1828)
First Anglo-Burmese War (Treaty of Yandabo, 1826), Barrackpore Mutiny (1824).
Annexation of Assam and parts of Burma.
Expansion into Northeast India; early indicators of sepoy grievance over overseas deployment.
Lord William Bentinck (1828–1833 as GG of Bengal)
Abolition of Sati (1829), suppression of Thuggee, Charter Act of 1833 (became first GG of India), Macaulays Minutes on Education (1835).
Annexation of Mysore (1831) on grounds of misgovernance, Treaty of Perpetual Friendship with Sindh.
Social reform era, welfare-oriented paternalistic administration, legal equality.

items.definition: Civil and criminal courts established at the district level by Warren Hastings in 1772 to replace traditional executive-led justice with formal judicial structures.
A landmark legislative enactment that strictly separated revenue administration from judicial administration, stripping collectors of magisterial powers and subjecting government officials to courts.
Introduced by Lord Cornwallis in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa in 1793, fixing land revenue permanently with Zamindars recognized as landowners.

Imperialist mechanism devised by Lord Wellesley requiring Indian rulers to maintain British troops, station a British Resident at court, and surrender foreign policy control in exchange for military protection.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Bengal Presidency Hub**: Calcutta served as the apex imperial capital and commercial nerve center, controlling trade arteries along the Gangetic plain.
• **Southern Expansion (Madras & Mysore)**: Consolidation through the Carnatic and Mysore wars established British hegemony over the Deccan plateau.
• **Western & Central Frontiers**: Maratha territories and Oudh integrated through Subsidiary Alliances and military campaigns, securing strategic land routes.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Administrative over-centralization, corruption in private trade, peasant agrarian distress due to high revenue demands, and resistance from traditional elite.
• **Policy Interventions**: Codification of laws, establishment of covenanted civil services, introduction of modern police networks, and systematic educational reforms.

items.title: Mnemonic for Governor-Generals of Bengal (1773–1833)
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: "**H**astings **C**ornwallis, **S**hore **W**ellesley, **B**arlow **M**into, **H**astings **A**mherst, **B**entinck"
• **Decoded Meaning**: Warren Hastings -> Lord Cornwallis -> Sir John Shore -> Lord Wellesley -> Lord George Barlow -> Lord Minto I -> Lord Hastings -> Lord Amherst -> Lord William Bentinck.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly solves chronological ordering questions and match-the-following sets regarding wars and reforms.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Remember **C**ornwallis for **C**ivil Services & Permanent Settlement, **W**ellesley for **W**ar & Subsidiary Alliance, and **B**entinck for **B**enevolent social reforms (Sati abolition).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently confuses the designation 'Governor-General of Bengal' with 'Governor-General of India'. Remember that Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General of Bengal (1773), but Lord William Bentinck was the first Governor-General of India (1833).

Mains Value Addition: Evaluate the transition of Governor-Generals from merchant-administrators to imperial satraps. Quote historian Eric Stokes on how the Cornwallis system prioritized administrative stability and property rights over indigenous participatory governance.

keyTakeaways: The office evolved from the Regulating Act of 1773 to centralize British control over regional presidencies.
Land revenue settlements (Permanent Settlement) and judicial/police reforms under Cornwallis laid the steel frame of British administration.
Expansionist strategies like Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance and Lord Hastings' military campaigns completed British paramountcy across India by 1823.
